name: Thread-looping (minimal access multiple plane suspension)

lead: Minimal access multiple plane suspension is a thread-lift variant in which sutures are looped and anchored at chosen points to hold drooping tissue in a higher position. It is used for facial rejuvenation, giving a lifted look with a small access and short recovery.
A 2019 report of 103 thread lifts performed between 2014 and 2017 found most patients satisfied at three months.

paras: A surgeon places looped sutures across multiple tissue planes of the face, anchoring them at selected points. Patients are typically evaluated for satisfaction and complications after the procedure.
In the study, 12.6% of patients had palpable suture knots, about 7.9% persistent swelling, 2.9% facial dimpling and 5.8% slight asymmetry that was easily corrected.

angle.text: The procedure lifts drooping facial tissue with small access points and little downtime, giving a firmer-looking face.

lead: Minimal access multiple plane suspension (thread-looping) is a facial rejuvenation technique described in a 2019 Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open paper. It uses looped sutures reinforced by select anchoring points to suspend ptotic (drooping) tissues across several planes.[1]

The paper reported 103 thread lifts performed between 2014 and 2017, with satisfactory results in 88 of 103 patients (85.4%) at three months, and concluded that the method offers minimal downtime and satisfactory cosmetic results.[1]

paras: The technique places looped sutures in multiple planes and anchors them at selected points to hold tissues in a lifted position.[1] It belongs to the wider family of thread lifts, which use barbed threads to pull skin without removing it.[2]

In the 103-patient series, 85.4% judged the result satisfactory at three months. Palpable knots affected 12.6%, persistent swelling 7.88% and dimpling 2.9%; 5.8% had slight asymmetry that was easily corrected.[1]

Wikipedia notes that errors with non-absorbable threads are hard to reverse and quotes a cosmetic doctor describing thread lifts as potentially the most dangerous aesthetic procedure, while a BBC investigation raised concerns about short training courses.[2]
A single case series of 103 thread lifts reported satisfactory results in 85.4% of patients at three months and a low complication rate.[1] No controlled trials are listed.
